newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FOCUS - Are Venezuelan stocks set to overboil?
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Are Venezuelan stocks set to overboil?

text.p: Are Venezuelan stocks set to overboil after ratcheting up gains of over 21 percent in June alone? Or is there more to go?
"I think so," Morgan Stanley Dean Witter's Latin American equities analyst Jay Pelosky wrote Monday in a market commentary -- although not all agree.
Stocks smashed through technical ceilings to an eighth successive record close Monday with the 19-share .IBC index at 9,273.38, up more than five percent for the session.

Pelosky favors market leaders telephone company CANTV, and exchange benchmark Electricidad de Caracas which has rocketed ahead a stellar 20 percent in only four days, after it was awarded a 75 percent rate increase last Thursday, taking the bolsa up with it.
"That (tariff rise) is a total windfall, the stock could go up 30 percent more," said local InvestAnalysis stocks watcher Alex Dalmady.

But what is good for Electricidad -- namely a rise in rates that analysts say will make electricity more expensive in Venezuela than the U.S. -- is also bad for what many consider an already pricey market, especially those companies that do not generate their own electricity.
"On the basis of fundamentals, if you buy Electricidad, you should sell everything else," Dalmady said.

Despite bullish economic growth prospects of five percent plus for this year and the next, the market is "discounting growth that is expected, but has yet to materialize, and company earnings based on that growth, without the smallest indication of them," Dalmady cautioned, adding that the looming earnings season could provide a useful reality check.
Rafael Alcantara, president of leading local brokerage Cavelba, agrees.
"The market is euphoric and overheated ... some (share) prices are at irrational levels ... the rally will last only as long as foreign interest does," he said.

So far, that interest looks like it's here to stay, spurred by the success of the third round of marginal oil field auctions that netted the country over $2 billion in the first week of June, plus a ground- breaking $8 billion labor market reform signed into law June 19.
"There's definitely been a surge of interest," said New York based-Credit Lyonnais broker Peter Ryan.

Further down the line, the market will benefit from the Chilean-style pension funds due to be set up under the Labor reform. As workers switch their funds to privately-run pensions scheme, demand for stocks in Venezuela's relatively small market should only increase, economists say.
The bolsa, which started the year as the region's worst-performing after more than doubling in real terms in 1996, is now up over 35 percent in the year.
"The bolsa's risen in six months what I had expected for the year, so God knows what happens now," Dalmady said.
Investment house Santander expects the IBC index to rise by 32 percent in dollar terms in 1997 and a whopping 84 percent over the coming 18 months.
